Course: Algorithms (week 9, topic: greedy versus dynamic programming, status: KNOWN).

Question: For the Algorithms revision sheet on greedy versus dynamic programming: explain greedy versus dynamic programming and say what actually decides the outcome. Where does this answer stop being right?

Student answer: It is only correct when the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure.

Official rubric points:
1. Says greedy commits to a local best choice and never revisits
2. Says greedy needs a proof or a property to be correct
3. Says DP explores overlapping subproblems and stores results
4. Gives a case where greedy fails and DP does not

Verdict: partially_correct. You earn 1 of 4; here is exactly where the other 3 went.

Earned, quoted from your answer:
- Point 2 (Says greedy needs a proof or a property to be correct): "it is only correct when the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure"

Not earned, because nothing in your answer covers them:
- Point 1: Says greedy commits to a local best choice and never revisits
- Point 3: Says DP explores overlapping subproblems and stores results
- Point 4: Gives a case where greedy fails and DP does not

The idea that needs replacing: that greedy and dynamic programming are two speeds of the same method, so greedy is simply the quicker one to write.
The correct statement: Test the greedy choice against a counterexample before trusting it: if swapping a later choice can improve an earlier commitment, you need DP.
Why: Greedy is only safe when a locally optimal choice is provably part of some global optimum; otherwise an early commitment closes off the branch that held the better answer.

Do this next: Run your greedy coin-change on denominations 1, 3 and 4 for targets 6 to 12, list every target where it is suboptimal, and then write the DP recurrence.

COD answers a trust problem - the buyer does not have to trust the seller or the payment channel - and it does so by moving risk onto the seller, who ships and pays for delivery before receiving anything. The clauses run in a logical order: FROM, then WHERE on individual rows, then GROUP BY, then HAVING on the resulting groups, then SELECT, then ORDER BY. That is why an aggregate cannot appear in WHERE - it does not exist yet - and why every non-aggregated selected column must be in GROUP BY. Filtering early in WHERE is also usually faster, since fewer rows reach the grouping step.

The classic is read-modify-write: two threads read the same value, both compute the same successor, and one update is lost. Reproducibility is a red herring - the interleaving is rare under test load and common under production load. Fixes remove the interleaving: a mutex around the critical section, an atomic operation, or a design where one owner mutates the state and others send it messages.

Question: Before the Web Application Development test, grade this for me. Set out accessible markup and the condition where it breaks. Be strict.

Student answer: Use heading elements instead of styled divs, because that is cleaner markup.

Official rubric points:
1. Says semantic elements convey structure to assistive technology
2. Says images need alternative text describing purpose
3. Says colour alone must not carry meaning
4. Says keyboard operation must work

Verdict: partially_correct - 1 of 4 points.

Credit where it is due: the conclusion is the one I would reach. "Use heading elements instead of styled divs, because that is cleaner markup." lands on the right action.
Not earned: the justification is what the rubric is marking, and yours does not hold - tidiness is a side benefit; the reason is that headings are how a screen-reader user navigates the page.

Named plainly, the wrong idea is this: that accessibility is an appearance setting added at the end, rather than structure that has to be in the markup from the start.
The fix, concretely: Put the structure in the markup - headings, labels, landmarks, alt text - because assistive technology reads structure, not appearance.
Why: A screen reader builds its navigation from the element tree, so a visually obvious heading that is a styled div does not exist as a heading at all.

To prove the fix stuck: Navigate your page with the keyboard only and with a screen reader's heading list, and write down everything you could not reach or identify.

Accessibility is structural. Assistive technology consumes the element tree: headings give a navigable outline, labels bind text to inputs, landmarks let a user skip to main content, alt text conveys what an image means. None of that is visible styling, which is why it cannot be bolted on at the end by adjusting colours. The quickest honest test is keyboard-only operation plus a heading list; both take minutes and catch most of it.

A screen reader builds its navigation from the element tree, so a visually obvious heading that is a styled div does not exist as a heading at all.

Question: explain density-independent layout well enough that someone could act on it. This is for Mobile Computing week 3. Tell me what is missing before I submit it.

Student answer: I set the button to 48 pixels because it looked right on my phone, so it will be the same size on every device.

Official rubric points:
1. Says physical pixels differ per device density
2. Says layout units are density independent
3. Says the system scales assets by density bucket
4. Says touch targets have a minimum physical size

Verdict: incorrect (0/4). Nothing here matches the rubric, so let us fix the idea rather than the wording.

Not earned: all 4 points. Your answer says "I set the button to 48 pixels because it looked right on my phone, so it will be the same size on every device." - and none of the rubric points can be read into that.

Named plainly, the wrong idea is this: that a pixel is a fixed physical size, so a layout that looks right on one phone is right everywhere.
The correction: Specify sizes in density-independent units and supply assets per density bucket, so the control keeps its physical size on every screen.
The mechanism: The system multiplies density-independent units by the device's scale factor, which is exactly what keeps a 48-unit target the same physical size on a dense and a sparse screen.

Do this next: Render your layout on two emulated densities, measure the button in millimetres on each, and correct whichever one is under the minimum.

Either I'm going crazy or Python is broken. I have: def add_task(task, tasks=[]): tasks.append(task); return tasks. First call: add_task('buy milk') returns ['buy milk']. Fine. LATER, a completely separate call add_task('study') returns ['buy milk', 'study']!! Where did buy milk COME FROM? A brand-new default list should be empty! Stack Overflow says write tasks=None then if tasks is None: tasks = [] inside, and it works, but nobody explains WHY the normal way is haunted.

Not crazy, not broken — you've stepped on Python's most famous rake, and the fix will make sense the moment you answer one question precisely: the expression [] in your def line — WHEN does Python execute it? Three candidates: (a) every time the function is called without tasks, (b) once, at the moment the def statement itself runs, (c) once per script. Design an experiment to find out — you have print, id(), and function attributes to work with.

Experiment: print(id(tasks)) inside the function, call it twice without the argument... same id both times. Same OBJECT. And actually — I remember __defaults__: print(add_task.__defaults__) shows (['buy milk'],) after the first call. The default list is sitting there ON the function, already containing my old task! So the answer is (b): [] runs ONCE when def executes, the resulting list is stored on the function object, and every no-argument call hands me THAT SAME list. My appends weren't going into fresh lists — they were accumulating in one list that lives as long as the function does.

You've just seen the whole mechanism with your own eyes — def is an executable statement, defaults are evaluated at def time and stored on the function, and calls REUSE the stored objects. Now the sharp question that separates understanding from folklore: why did nobody warn you about def greet(name, punctuation='!')? That default is also evaluated once and shared. Why is the string harmless while your list was haunted?

I think the filesystem is corrupted. The disk hit 100%, I found the culprit — a 30GB app.log — and deleted it with rm. It's GONE, ls shows nothing. But df STILL says 100% full! And here's the crazy part: du on the whole disk adds up to 30GB LESS than what df reports used. The numbers don't agree with each other. Before I reformat, is there any way to fix a filesystem this broken?

Do not reformat — your filesystem isn't broken, and the 30GB disagreement between du and df is not noise; it's a precise clue, because those two tools count DIFFERENT things. du walks the directory tree adding up files it can reach by name. df asks the filesystem how many blocks are allocated, reachable or not.

I assumed rm deletes the file — data and all. But given the evidence... it removed the NAME, the directory entry, and the data blocks are somehow still allocated. Is that why the syscall is called unlink and not delete? Like the name is just a link to the actual file?

You've just read a decades-old design decision straight out of a syscall name — yes. In Unix filesystems, a file IS an inode: the data blocks plus metadata, identified by number. A directory entry is merely a name pointing at an inode, and one inode can have many names (hard links).

An open file descriptor! The app that WRITES app.log — it's still running, and it opened that log file ages ago. It doesn't care about the name; it holds a handle straight to the inode. So the kernel keeps the inode alive because the process might still read or write it... and in fact my app is probably STILL WRITING to the deleted file right now, growing those invisible 30GB even bigger. That's why the disk stays full!

Exactly — the inode's lifetime is governed by a reference count: link count (names) plus open handles, and the blocks free only when BOTH hit zero. Your rm took the link count to zero, but one open handle keeps the corpse warm — and yes, still growing.

The blunt way: restart the app — the handle closes on exit, references hit zero, 30GB frees instantly. Gentler... could I empty the file through the handle instead of removing it? Like truncate the still-open file to zero bytes? If the app has the file open, there must be a path to it through the process — /proc maybe?

Both correct, and the second is the professional's move: `truncate -s 0 /proc/PID/fd/N` — or better, BEFORE deleting next time, `truncate -s 0 app.log` or `> app.log`, which empties the data while keeping the same inode, so the app's handle stays valid and the space frees immediately.

My caching layer has a bug. I added Redis in front of our product database — pages went from 800ms to 40ms, huge win — but now marketing updates a price and customers keep seeing the OLD price for like an hour. Where's the bug in my cache code — some kind of sync flag I forgot?

Read your own description again, slowly: the cache returns what you stored, for as long as you told it to (your TTL is 3600 seconds, I'd bet). It's not malfunctioning — it's keeping the exact promise you wrote. Here's the reframe you need before touching code: a cache is a DEAL. You traded 760ms of latency for something. What did you pay? Name the currency.

I paid... freshness. The 40ms page is fast because it skips the database — which means it can't know the database changed. So 'cache bug' is the wrong frame: staleness isn't a defect, it's the price tag. But then how is caching ever safe? Different data must tolerate different amounts of staleness... product DESCRIPTIONS being an hour old is fine, prices being an hour old costs money and maybe legal trouble.

You just did the analysis most teams skip: a staleness budget per data type. Description: hours are fine. Price: minutes at most, arguably seconds. Stock count: seconds, or customers buy things you don't have. So the design question becomes: for data with a TINY staleness budget, how do you keep cache speed without waiting for the TTL to expire? The update event itself is your resource — marketing SAVED a new price; your system knows the exact moment truth changed. Use it.

My caching layer has a bug. I added Redis in front of our product database — pages went from 800ms to 40ms, huge win — but now marketing updates a price and customers keep seeing the OLD price for like an hour. Where's the bug in my cache code — some kind of sync flag I forgot?

Read your own description again, slowly: the cache returns what you stored, for as long as you told it to (your TTL is 3600 seconds, I'd bet). It's not malfunctioning — it's keeping the exact promise you wrote. Here's the reframe you need before touching code: a cache is a DEAL. You traded 760ms of latency for something. What did you pay? Name the currency.

I paid... freshness. The 40ms page is fast because it skips the database — which means it can't know the database changed. So 'cache bug' is the wrong frame: staleness isn't a defect, it's the price tag. But then how is caching ever safe? Different data must tolerate different amounts of staleness... product DESCRIPTIONS being an hour old is fine, prices being an hour old costs money and maybe legal trouble.

You just did the analysis most teams skip: a staleness budget per data type. Description: hours are fine. Price: minutes at most, arguably seconds. Stock count: seconds, or customers buy things you don't have. So the design question becomes: for data with a TINY staleness budget, how do you keep cache speed without waiting for the TTL to expire? The update event itself is your resource — marketing SAVED a new price; your system knows the exact moment truth changed. Use it.

Invalidate on write! When the price-update endpoint commits to the database, it also deletes (or overwrites) that product's cache entry — the next reader misses, fetches fresh, repopulates. Staleness window shrinks from an hour to milliseconds. But that couples my update path to the cache... and what about updates that don't go through my endpoint, like the bulk CSV import marketing runs?

And THERE is why cache invalidation is famously one of the two hard problems: every write path must remember to invalidate, forever, including the bulk import someone writes next year. Your defense in layers: (1) invalidate-on-write for the paths you control; (2) a SHORT TTL as the safety net — not an hour but 60 seconds for prices — so any forgotten write path self-heals in a minute instead of never; (3) route writes through one place (a repository layer or DB trigger/change stream) so 'remember to invalidate' lives in one file, not in every developer's head.
